newsitem.title: USA: U.S. to relax computer code export restrictions.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to relax computer code export restrictions.

text.p: The Clinton administration unveiled on Tuesday its long-awaited policy to relax export restrictions on computer encoding technology, a critical component of global communications and online commerce.

But the proposal did little to mollify critics of the current restrictions in Congress and the software industry who argue that foreign competitors not subject to any limits are cleaning up in the encryption business.

"It will support the growth of electronic commerce, increase the security of global information and sustain the economic competitiveness of U.S. encryption product manufacturers," U.S. Vice President Al Gore said.

Encryption programmes use mathematical formulas to scramble information, such as an electronic mail message or a credit card number sent over the Internet, and render it unreadable without a password or software key.
Under current law, U.S. companies can only export programmes using short keys, 40 bits of computer data, which can be easily cracked by a determined hacker.
The new plan would allow companies to export programmes with 56 bit long keys if the companies agreed to include so-called key recovery features within two years.
With key recovery, the government can gain access to duplicate keys with a court order or similiar authorisation, similiar to the process for obtaining a wiretap.
The key length limit would not apply to programmes once key recovery was added and use of encryption in the United States would continue to be unregulated.

Also under the plan, a presidential executive order to be signed in a few weeks, oversight of the review process for granting export licenses would be moved to the Commerce Department from the State Department.
In Congress, which considered this year but did not pass two bills nearly abolishing all export restrictions, reaction to the Clinton plan was restrained but critical.

"I can't say I'm pleased with a process that has all but excluded Congress," said Sen. Conrad Burns, primary sponsor of one of the bills. "The debate is not over by any stretch," the Montana Republican said, adding he planned to reintroduce his bill next year.
Software makers were less restrained. "It's wrong headed and it's going backwards," Peter Harter, public policy counsel at Netscape Communications Corp, said.
Netscape is losing millions of dollars in sales overseas on its Internet products to foreign competitors who are not bound by U.S. export laws, Harter said.
But intelligence and law enforcement officials fear widespread use of strong encryption will cripple their efforts to catch drug dealers, terrorists and other criminals.

"The battleground is to allow people to have access to secure electronic communication, on the one hand, balanced against legitimate law enforcement interests," said John Deutch, director of the Central Intelligence agency.

Deutch said even drug cartels that could theoretically obtain powerful encryption illegally generally used off-the-shelf communications equipment. "If you allow easy access to encryption, you make the problem of interdicting drugs more serious," Deutch said.

Not all agree the Clinton plan is properly balanced. "Clearly it places the needs of law enforcement above the needs personal privacy and the needs of business," said Shabbir Safdar, a privacy advocate with the Voters Telecommunications Watch.
